If there's an outstanding balance, use the pay now option to retry the charge immediately. After saving changes, refresh Ads Manager and give it a couple of minutes to sync. You should see the error clear once payment is confirmed. That's it. By going to Meta Business Suite, opening Ads Manager, heading to billing and payments, reviewing payment settings, and then verifying or readding your payment method, you can resolve the most common account errors quickly and get your campaigns back on Back.

They target very specific local audiences (e.g., homeowners in ZIP codes 07650–07660, age 35–65, interests in "home improvement" + "recently moved")
They use lead forms + Messenger + call extensions so people can book instantly
They have good reviews, real photos of work, fast response time (under 5 minutes)
They track everything (call tracking, pixel, CRM) and cut losing ads fast
They usually run retargeting + lookalike audiences off past customers

If you’re doing none of the above and just posting in groups or running $20 broad ads, of course you get zero leads. Facebook isn’t magic — it’s a paid traffic machine.
3. Why you’re probably not getting leads (most common reasons)

Ads too broad (showing to everyone instead of homeowners in your town)
Bad creative (stock photos, long captions, no clear "call me now" button)
Landing page/form sucks (slow, ugly, asks too many questions)
You reply to leads in 2 hours instead of 2 minutes
No budget consistency (Facebook punishes stop-start spending)
No reviews or trust signals (people won’t call a blank profile)
Targeting wrong people (renters, teenagers, out-of-area)

4. Real numbers from actual service businesses (2025–2026)

Average cost per lead (CPL) for local services: $15–$60
Average customer value: $300–$3,000+ (one job)
Good ROI: 3–10× return on ad spend
Example: Spend $1,000/month → get 20–50 leads → close 5–15 jobs → make $5,000–$30,000 revenue

Many real businesses quietly make $10k–$50k+/month from Facebook ads — they just don’t post screenshots every day.

But, two things we do need to talk about are the buying types and the campaign objective. So, we've got two different buying types. We've got auction, and we've got reservation. Auction is just the cost of your Facebook and Instagram ads is going to be determined by simple market forces, demand and supply. More demand, higher cost. Less demand, lower cost. And that's demand from advertisers, by the way. How many advertisers there are, how much they're willing to spend. Uh reservation, you can actually guarantee a certain price, often a lower price. And and the cost of Facebook and Instagram advertising is normally measured in CPMs. So, cost per 1,000 impressions. So, it's cheaper to use reservation, but that's not the option I'd recommend you use, which might sound bizarre. Here's why. In order for Meta to be able to guarantee that lower cost, they are going to put your ads in front of lower quality prospects, or lower quality ad placements. Awareness is where Meta will put your ads in front of people that are most likely to remember them. Put your ads in front of as many people as possible. Not an option I typically recommend for beginners or for businesses operating with a relatively small Facebook and Instagram ad budget because it can be quite an easy way in those scenarios to spend a bunch of money and not really see anything back for it. What we see with awareness is it can work really well for larger businesses with big budgets because awareness takes time and it takes a lot of ad impressions across a lot of people over an extended period. Bigger businesses have those budgets, smaller ones and beginners to to Meta ads typically don't. If your business account uses a different address than your bank account, that mismatch can trigger declines. If everything looks right, but payments are still failing, contact your bank. Ask whether there are any blocks, insufficient funds, daily limits, or restrictions on online or international transactions. Some banks automatically flag charges from advertising platforms for security reasons. So, request that they allow charges from Meta or Facebook. If your card uses additional verification like one-time passwords, confirm that online payments are enabled. If needed, try a different payment method. In payment settings, add another valid card or supported alternative like a digital wallet where available. Set the new method as your primary and remove any expired or invalid cards. Uh, keep your billing country and currency consistent with your ad account to avoid errors. and be aware that a small temporary authorization may appear when you add a new card. Finally, update and save your payment information. After saving, return to billing to see if the outstanding balance clears. Facebook may retry the charge automatically, and after a successful payment, your ads should resume delivery. That's it. By confirming your details, checking with your bank, trying a different method, and updating your payment settings, you can quickly resolve most payment failures in Ads Manager. You're probably scratching your head thinking, "Well, yeah, that's where I want to send people. What's wrong with that?" Well, there's nothing wrong with it, but you actually want to send people to the landing page, so the actual shopping page on your website instead of the homepage. And the reason for that is because you want to remove as much friction in the buying process as possible. If you send people to the website, maybe they'll get confused. And then go ahead and click apply. But if you have no clue what you're looking for when it comes to should I scale or should I kill my ad campaign, then listen carefully. Cost per acquisition or your CPA is king. The first thing that you need to do is you need to determine how much you can spend on your ads to profitably acquire a new customer. And to do that, the formula is quite simple. So to find your break even CPA, you take the average order value on your store and you multiply that by the gross margin. So, let's say that every time a customer buys from your store, on average, you get $60 in revenue. And let's say that your gross margin is 60%. So, basically, 40% of that $60 you have to spend on fulfilling the product. Then, all you have to do is take the $60, multiply it by 60%, and you find out that your break even CPA is $36. Now, the rule of thumb here is if your CPA is below break even, so you're profitable, then you want to scale carefully. If your CPA is 10 to 20% above break even, so maybe it's costing you $40 to get a purchase, then you're in the optimization window. If your CPA is way above break even and you're just not acquiring customers or customers are costing you hundreds of dollars in spend, then kill the campaign. Another key metric you should be looking at is the 3second view rate. So generally on Facebook, you want to look for 30% or more. That's quite strong and it shows you that people are really engaging with your ads and the content you've created is interesting. If it's 20 to 30% workable, but it could probably use some more optimization or changes. And if it's below 20%, that's a good indication that it's a bad ad. Next, you have CTR or click-through rate. So, this is the percentage of people that see your ad and then decide to click on it and go to your website. Generally, looking at 1.5% and above is quite healthy. If you're below that or under 1%, then you should definitely optimize or start making new ads. It's likely that you have a bad angle or a weak offer. Another metric to keep in mind is your CPC or your cost per click. So, if the CTR is high, meaning that tons of people are clicking on your ad, but the cost per click is also high, then maybe it's a targeting mismatch and your ads are just going to the wrong people or you're in a super competitive market and you should probably switch the marketing angle and try to find a new customer avatar. If the CTR is very low and the CPC is also high, then that just tells you it's a bad creative and it's costing you a ton of money to drive any kind of clicks. Now, I could go on and on about all the different metrics that you could read, but remember, CPA is king, and you want to make sure your creative is good by looking at the 3-se secondond view rate as well as the CTR and how the CTR compares with the CPC. In order to efficiently run Facebook ads, you first need to understand what Facebook ads really are. What are Facebook ads? More than two billion people use Facebook every single month. Advertisers bid to show their ad on those people's devices. Facebook advertising is simply an online auction. Each time there's an opportunity to show someone an ad, an auction takes place to determine which advertiser will have the chance to show their ad. Billions of auctions take place every single day across the Facebook family of apps and network of websites. When we as advertisers create ads, we tell Facebook who we want to show our ads to by defining a target audience. A person can fall into multiple target audiences. For example, one advertiser targets women who like skiing, while another advertiser targets all skiers who live in California. the same person, in this case a female skier who lives in California, could fall into the target audience of both of the advertisers. So now, when there's an opportunity to show that single person an ad and there's multiple advertisers targeting them, those advertisers will now enter an auction where they will bid to show their creative on that user's device. So, how do you win an auction? To ensure that the winning ad maximizes value for both people and the business, the winner of the auction is the ad with the highest total value. And this is extremely extremely important to take note of. The highest total value is a combination of three major factors. Number one, the bid. The bid is placed by an advertiser for that ad placement. In other words, what is the advertiser willing to pay to achieve their desired outcome? There's actually multiple ways to manage your bid in an ad auction. We'll discuss this later on in the course, but for now, the first key of a highest total value is the bid. What amount is the advertiser willing to pay to show their ad to that user on their device? Number two, estimated action rates. An estimate of whether a particular person engages with or converts from a particular ad. In other words, the probability that showing an ad to a person leads to that desired outcome of the advertiser. For example, if your goal is a purchase, what is the estimated probability that if Facebook shows your ad, that user will result in a purchase? Finally, number three, ad quality. Ad quality is a measure of the quality of an ad as determined from many sources including feedback from people viewing or hiding the ad and assessments of lowquality attributes in the ad such as withholding information, sensationalized language, and engagement bait. And a big takeaway is that engaging in clickbait and engagement bait does not improve ad performance. So together, these estimated action rates and ad quality measure the ad relevance. In fact, Facebook subsidizes relevant ads in auctions. So, more relevant ads actually cost less and see more results. In other words, an ad that's relevant to a person could win an auction against ads with higher bids. And this is a big trend that we've been seeing over the past few years with Facebook. After they got in some trouble with the government and ca with the Cambridge Analytica scheme, they became quote unquote more transparent with their users. And a big piece of that was making the user's experience on Facebook better. And so as advertisers, by creating a good experience for the user and a good experience through to Facebook by driving results, it's a win-win. And Facebook will actually charge you less to show your ad more against people that are trying to outbid you. So how do you know if your ad performed against those three mention criterias? There's actually a way to view in the ads manager, but once again, we're going to get into that later on in the course. As you just learned, there's a lot more to Facebook ads. So, how does Facebook collect data based on actions that we're taking off of the Facebook application and network of sites? Well, they use what's called a pixel. The Facebook pixel is what allows Facebook to track user engagement, actions, checkouts, etc. off of their platform. So, what is the pixel? Well, the pixel is simply a piece of JavaScript code that is put onto your web pages that loads when a specific action is taken. Luckily, if you use Shopify or WordPress or any of the really majority of e-commerce and website builders, they have an easy integration to quickly set up your pixel so you don't have to touch any code whatsoever. As I said, the Facebook pixel, a piece of code for your website that lets you measure, optimize, and build audiences for your ad campaigns. So, measure cross device conversions. For example, without a pixel, how would Facebook know that maybe someone started checking out on their computer but finished the checkout on their phone? They wouldn't be able to do that without the pixel. So with the pixel, you can measure someone that checks out or starts a checkout on one device and finishes the purchase on a different one. Optimize delivery to people likely to take action. As Facebook collects data on your potential customer base, they're then able to utilize that data to show your ads to people that are more likely to purchase than not. The more data that you can give Facebook, the better. The pixel enables this. Create custom audiences from website visitors. When we get to the lessons that discuss retargeting, we're going to be utilizing the data from the pixel to to break out this bulk audience into separate ones. For example, we might want to target people that viewed a specific product or added a specific product to cart or purchased something in the last 7 days. We can do all of that because of the pixel. This also enables us, the pixel also enables us to create dynamic ads. One really cool feature about Facebook is they can take different pieces of media. For example, they can take a different image or video, combine it with different text, and show it to a customer because they know that they viewed a specific product from the data on the pixel. And then finally, learn about your website traffic. You can get demographic breakdown, audience breakdowns, understand what website pages people visited, what website uh pages people left or bounced on, and really break it down. How the Facebook pixel works. Well, as I mentioned, when someone visits your website and then takes a action, for example, the example here, buying something or even viewing a piece of content or clicking the add to car button, the Facebook pixel is triggered and reports this action back to Facebook. This way, you know when a customer took an action after seeing your Facebook ad. And you'll also be able to reach that customer again by using the custom audience, which we're going to discuss how to do in a later lesson. When more and more conversions happen on your website, Facebook gets better at delivering your ad to people who are more likely to take certain actions. And that's called conversion optimization. While the Koreans shower you with features, and the Europeans focus on dynamics and feel, the Japanese bring something else to the table. Quiet functionality. This Honda City facelift hasn't moved the goalpost or upset the status quo. It has however injected some muchneeded attitude into what remains the most dependable and sensible sedan in the midsize segment.

- How to Use Facebook Ads Automated Rules (2026 Guide): Kind: captions Language: en In today's video, I'm going to teach you how to use Facebook ads automated rules. If you've ever wished your ads could adjust themselves while you sleep, automated rules are your best friend. They help you enforce performance guardrails, scale winners, and cut waste without constant manual checks. First, head to Facebook Ads Manager. Make sure you're in the correct ad account so you're seeing the right campaigns and data. From the sidebar, click all tools, then choose automated rules. This is the dedicated area where you'll create, view, and manage all rules tied to your campaigns. Select create rule to start a new one. This opens a setup panel where you'll define exactly what the rule should watch and what it should do when conditions are met. Give your rule a descriptive name. Clarity here saves you later. A simple formula works well. Objective or metric, level, condition, and action. For example, CPA, adset, pause, cost per result, 30, daily. Names like this make it easy to scan your list and understand the purpose at a glance. Next, choose what you want the rule to apply to. You can target all active campaigns, specific campaigns, ad sets, or individual ads. If you're testing multiple creatives, applying rules at the ad level is helpful. If you're controlling spend, the ad set or campaign level often makes more sense. Pick only what you truly want automated. Broad selections can have wide reaching effects. Now, define the action. This is what happens when your conditions are met. Common actions include pausing underperformers, turning items on, increasing or decreasing budgets by a set amount or percentage, or sending a notification so you can review manually. Keep actions proportional for budget changes. Small percentage adjustments help avoid big swings. Choose the metrics and thresholds that trigger the rule. Popular choices are cost per result greater than a target, or OS below a minimum, frequency too high, or spend over a limit with few results. Select an appropriate time window like last 3 days or last 7 days to smooth out short-term volatility. Make sure your metric aligns with your campaign objective for reliable signals. Decide how often the rule checks and applies. You can run it continuously, hourly, or on a daily schedule. Consider data delays. For conversion metrics, less frequent checks with a longer look back can be more accurate. For spend or frequency, hourly checks may be fine. When everything looks good, click create. Your rule is now live and will monitor performance based on your settings.

- The NEW BEST Facebook Ads Campaign Structure for 2026: Kind: captions Language: en If your Facebook ads used to work at first, driving leads and sales, but now have flatlined, or if you never really felt like they got off the ground to begin with, the problem is usually not your ads, your product, your targeting, or even the algorithm. It's probably your account structure. Most small businesses launch a few campaigns, throw all their ads into one place, and then try to scale. At first, it works, but as you add more creatives, more audiences, and more budget, everything starts interfering with everything else. New ads reset that learning, winning ads lose spend, retargeting overlaps with prospecting, and the algorithm stops performing predictably. And if that sounded a little confusing, let me put it this way. The brands that scale consistently, whether they're spending $100 a day or $10,000 a day, almost always have one thing in common. They run a structured system that separates acquisition, testing, scaling, retargeting, and retention. In this video, I'm going to break down the new best Facebook ads campaign structure for 2026, designed specifically around how Meta's algorithm works right now. We'll walk through five key components. The main campaign, where most of your budget goes, the scaling campaign, where winners get pushed harder, interest testing without confusing the algorithm, retargeting people who showed interest but didn't buy, and retention campaigns that turn customers into repeat buyers, if that makes sense given the nature of your business. So, even if you've never had real success with Facebook ads before, by the end of this video, you will know the exact steps to take to manage, scale, and optimize your ads for leads and sales. And in case you don't know, I'm Brandy with Life Marketing, the digital marketing agency with a mission to help small businesses grow. We've helped small businesses go from zero to thousands in revenue coming in every month from [music] social media. If you just want to see how we could do the same for your business with no strings attached, click the link below to schedule a free strategy call. Otherwise, we're going to jump in with the first of five steps on how to best structure your Facebook ads campaign, starting with step one, set up your main prospecting campaign. The foundation of almost every successful Facebook ad account is a single main prospecting campaign focused entirely on acquiring brand new customers. This campaign should usually receive around 80% of your total ad spend. If you're spending $100 a day, that means roughly $80 should go here. If you're spending $1,000 a day, roughly $800 goes here. The reason is simple. This campaign is responsible for bringing new people into your ecosystem, which fuels everything else in your account. So, if this campaign isn't set up correctly and drawing the right people in, the rest of the steps in this video won't matter. Inside this campaign, you want to keep everything as simple as possible, so you want to use a sales objective if you want sales, or the lead objective if you want leads. Set it on campaign budget optimization, so that it will distribute your budget in real time to the best performing ad sets, meaning you don't have to manually do that yourself all the time. And choose broad targeting. Meta's algorithm is smart enough now to read your ad copy, your creative, your destination URL, and find the right audience based on those things. It no longer needs you to enter in a bunch of detailed targeting options like interests and behaviors to figure out who to show the ad to. If anything, you can enter in age, gender, and location if any of those things truly matter for your business, like if you only service a certain local radius, or if your product is exclusively for women, etc. Otherwise, instead of narrowing audiences with dozens of interests, you're allowing the algorithm to do the work. However, there is one important rule here. For this campaign, you should exclude people who already know your brand. That means creating a custom audience of recent website visitors or social media engagers, add-to-cart users, and existing customers. And then once you've created that audience, exclude that audience in the ad set level. This ensures the campaign focuses only on true new customer acquisition. Now, the key structural element inside this campaign is something called creative packs. Each time you launch a new round of ads, you place them into a separate ad set pack. For example, broad pack one, broad pack two, broad pack three. Each pack contains a different batch of creatives. This system prevents new ads from interfering with older ads that are already performing well. So, instead of constantly resetting Meta's learning phase, each pack, or ad set, gathers its own data independently. And over time, your prospecting campaign becomes a structured testing environment where new creative enters the system without disrupting existing winners. Once you identify ads that perform extremely well, those ads graduate to the next stage, which leads us to step two, set up the scale campaign. Your second campaign exists for one purpose, scaling proven winners. So, this campaign is where you duplicate your best performing ads from the first campaign and allow the algorithm to push more budget behind them. Think of this campaign is your high-performance engine. Inside your prospecting campaign, many ads will run. Some will fail. Some will perform decently. But a few ads will consistently generate strong results. When you find those winners, you duplicate them into your scale campaign. This campaign should only contain ads that have already proven they can generate conversions profitably. The structure here, again, stays simple. One campaign, one broad audience, and only winning ads. The algorithm then pushes budget towards the strongest performers. This setup prevents new experimental creative from interfering with ads that are already working. And again, instead of constantly resetting Meta's learning phase, you allow proven ads to scale efficiently in their own environment. Once your winners are scaling, the next step is learning more about your audience with step three, interest testing. Even though broad targeting performs extremely well today, interest testing can still provide valuable insights. However, most advertisers test interests incorrectly. They test new audiences and new creatives at the same time, which makes it impossible to understand what actually caused the performance change. Instead, the correct approach is to test interests using proven ads only. In other words, the creative is already validated, and it has already shown to work. So, now the audience becomes the variable. For example, if you sell fitness apparel, you might test audiences like CrossFit, Gymshark, or Nike Training Club. Each interest is placed in its own ad set, but all of them use the exact same proven winning ads. This allows you to clearly see whether the audience itself improves performance. Sometimes an interest group reveals a pocket of buyers the algorithm was not prioritizing before. And occasionally, those insights feed back into your broad targeting performance as Meta learns more about the ideal customer profile. Interest testing is not the core driver of performance anymore, but it remains a valuable way to expand reach strategically. Once new prospects enter your ecosystem, the next step is converting those who showed interest but didn't buy. So, step four, set up your retargeting campaign. Not everyone buys the first time they see your product. In fact, most people don't. On average, it takes seven interactions with a brand before a customer will make a purchase. That's why every account needs a dedicated retargeting campaign. This campaign focuses exclusively on people who have already interacted with your brand. So, typical retargeting audiences include website visitors from the last 30 days, people who added products to their cart, and social media engagers. These audiences already know who you are, which means your messaging should look a little different from the first two campaigns. Instead of introducing the brand, retargeting ads should focus on reminding people about products they viewed, showing social proof, addressing objections, and highlighting urgency or offers. The important rule here is that this campaign should only target these audiences. Meta sometimes tries to expand beyond retargeting audiences, which can cause spend to leak back into prospecting. So, to avoid this, make sure audience expansion settings are turned off, so the campaign stays tightly focused. Retargeting campaigns typically run with smaller budgets than prospecting campaigns, but they often produce some of the highest conversion rates in your account, because this is your warmer audience. Once someone finally makes a purchase, the next opportunity begins. So, step five, drive repeat purchases with a retention campaign. Many advertisers make the mistake of treating a customer's first purchase as the end of the buying journey, but in reality, it's just the beginning. Your retention campaign exists to turn customers into repeat buyers. This campaign targets only people who have already purchased from your brand before. However, not all customers are the same. Someone who bought last week behaves very differently from someone who bought a year ago. That's why retention should usually be split into two audiences. First is recent buyers, typically customers from the last 180 days. These people already remember your brand, so your ads can focus on complimentary products, upsells, or new releases. And then the second one, older buyers, customers who purchased further in the past. These audiences may need reminders on your brand overall, seasonal offers, or product updates to bring them back. Retention campaigns are extremely powerful because the cost of acquiring a repeat customer is usually much lower than acquiring a brand new one. When done correctly, they increase customer lifetime value and improve the overall profitability of your ad account. The reason this campaign structure works so well overall is that it separates different marketing objectives into their own environments. Your prospecting campaign focuses entirely on finding new customers. Your scaling campaign pushes winning ads harder. Interest testing allows you to explore new audiences without confusing the algorithm. Retargeting converts people who have already showed interest, and retention campaigns generate repeat purchases from existing customers. So, instead of one messy account where everything overlaps, you now have a system where each campaign has a clear purpose. And that clarity makes optimization easier, protects your best ads, maximizes your dollar, and gives Meta's algorithm cleaner signals to work with. If you implement this structure correctly, your ad account will get far easier to scale because every part of the system is designed to do one job extremely well. And it doesn't matter if you're spending $10 a day, $100 a day, $1,000 a day, or $20,000 a day. These are core principles, the same things that we use at The Moon Liters for our clients, no matter the size of the brand. The first major shift is one that is real. This is not observation. This is a shift that has happened. The old algorithm is now the new Andromeda algorithm. What we need to understand here is what is this shift? Why is it so important? And how are we adapting to it with structure first. So, first off, the Andromeda algorithm has been a shift from audience to creative targeting. Now, what this very simply means is in the old algorithm, you would choose your audience, whether it's broad, interest, lookalikes, whatever, and the creatives you push into that ad set get targeted from that interest group. This has now flipped. Instead of an interest or a broad target deciding who the ads are going to be shown to, that has completely reversed. We now have a situation where whatever ads are within your ad set define the targeting on an individual level. This means that, yes, you could have completely different ads in the same ad set that target two very different people. It also means that you could have multiple ad sets in the same campaign targeting completely different people, even if the targeting, the interest group, or the broad is 100% the same. Now, I don't want to get too conceptual on this, but what this means is that your creative concepts matter more than ever. And the structure that we actually like to deploy to solve for Andromeda that we've proven out across 80-plus accounts at this point is one of with swim lanes. Now, swim lanes are a very simple philosophy that we need to separate prospecting, retargeting, and retention. So, the important part about swim lanes is that you as the advertiser actually know where you're spending your money. One of the biggest flaws that we see with Facebook is that it overspends on engage and existing customers. It's fine to spend a lot of money on engage. It's fine to spend a lot of money on existing customers. But what I don't like is when advertisers or brands that we work with think that they're spending money on prospects. They think they're spending money on new customers when in reality, they're actually spending a boatload of that cash on existing and engage, which they believe they're targeting in other places like email, SMS, and other retargeting methods. What we like to do is make sure that our swim lanes are clearly defined. Our first swim lane is prospecting. This is generally a CBO prospecting campaign mixed with a boatload of ad sets. Those could be a combination of broad and interest groups, even lookalikes if you'd like to give them a shot. The important part is that we're grouping a lot together in one campaign, and we are creating a hyper-competitive environment. I want to actually say that twice. A hyper-competitive environment is one of the most important things that you could have in a Facebook ads account because you're actually giving the algorithm some power to decide where to spend your money. Now, this is very, very different than a one campaign method or just throwing everything into one ad set because you could actually define minimum, maximum budgets and even put exclusions on things at the ad set level within your prospecting campaigns. That's the control, that's the levers that we like to have on our side without just giving all the power to Facebook. The second and third swim lanes are retargeting and retention. Retargeting is anyone who's visited your site and anyone who's engaged with your business. They know about you, very simple. Retention, on the other hand, is anyone who's purchased. This isn't someone who's added to cart. This isn't someone who almost purchased. They've handed you money. That is a very big difference between retargeting and retention. We want to make sure we're treating each of these buckets separately, we're dedicating our budget accordingly, and even in some cases curating the creative to each of these buckets. But most of the time, it's okay to have the same creatives in each with a big testing environment in our prospecting CBO. And you might ask, why? Why does this fix Andromeda? Why does this fix the issue that everyone seems to have in the back of their mind? It's actually quite simple. It starts in the prospecting CBO campaign. The prospecting CBO campaign now has the capability to spend its cash wherever it wants, meaning your audiences can individually be targeted per creative. So, think about it like this. If you separated all of your ad sets or all of your creative concepts into different campaigns, then you're controlling the budget. $200 here, $200 here, $200 here. But grouping these together, what it actually does is it allows you to still see very clearly with organized ad sets, set minimums and maximum budgets if you need, and with your total budget, so 200, 200, 200 equaling 600 on a total CBO budget, Facebook will distribute wherever the cash is best spent. And I know one issue that a lot of people have is that certain creatives don't get any spend. I'm here to tell you this is a feature, not a bug, most of the time. Not all the time. Most of the time, Facebook is saving you cash by doing this. So, what I would advise, if you really feel like there's an ad that you've put a lot of time or effort into, set a minimum budget, make sure it gets $25, $50 a day, let it ramp up a little bit. If it doesn't work after 7 days, kill that minimum budget. Okay, so our structures are complete. The second shift that I have seen and that basically everyone has seen because it actually happened. This is not theoretical. The second shift that has happened in Facebook ads in the last year is massive changes to attribution and measurement. We all remember when the conversions API came out. Now, I want to challenge all of these third-party attribution softwares because they do have their place, but I think people get too excited about them when we actually have the best tool natively built into Facebook. And that is exactly what Meta is capable of doing with its standard attribution. It sounds so boring because it's built in, and there's fancy tools with great marketing slogans that actually sell us into programs that don't do as much as the actual Facebook tracking. And then it offers you all conversions or just the first conversion or both. So, we will go all and we will click apply. And you can see here that the return on ad spend just from the incremental attributions is actually 24. So, just over half. And the purchase conversion value is 68 and a half,000 pounds. It is nearly halfed our purchase conversion value. And the reason for that is it's looking at what sales would this client have made anyway. And then it's looking at what is the uplift that Facebook has made. So if Facebook wasn't there, they would have made £68.5,000 less sales. So, the reason we leave it off is because with the old attribution settings, you are making more sales. And I think it gives you a truer reflection of the actual impact and value your ads have had. Think about it. Incremental attribution is less likely to count conversions like that. Exactly how Facebook measure that, no one knows.
